title: Work redesign: Organisation captures more value than access
desc: Explains the implementation gap through integrated learning and coordination, while company cases cannot establish universal returns.

kps.k: The central proposition shifts AI advantage from tool adoption to the organisation of work.
kps.d: McKinsey, Tellmann, PwC and DORA argue that faster individual tasks do not automatically improve enterprise performance: unchanged handoffs, decision rights, data silos and incentives can absorb the gains. Their proposed alternative combines workflow redesign, integrated data, governance and talent development. McKinsey makes an important distinction: organisational capabilities enable valuable products, customer relationships and proprietary assets; redesign does not create value by itself.

qs.q: Most companies are using AI to accelerate existing activities while leaving the underlying operating model, including governance, teams, and capabilities, largely unchanged.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: - *Value remains trapped at the task level.* Individual activities become faster, but broader workflows do not.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Reported adoption and returns reveal an implementation gap, but the sources measure different outcomes.
kps.d: McKinsey reports that companies attributing at least 5% of EBIT to AI were three times more likely to pursue broad redesign. The Future of Professionals report associates visible AI strategies with twice the likelihood of AI-related revenue growth. Neither association establishes causation. The GenAI Divide, drawing on interviews, surveys and 300 public implementations, claims 95% of organisations receive zero return, while PwC says many obtain modest returns that exceed costs without transforming the business. These accounts differ in scope and outcome definitions; they do not establish a common failure rate. PwC supplies no quantified supporting cases in the excerpt.

qs.q: In fact, the McKinsey survey showed that top performers—companies attributing 5 percent or more of EBIT to AI—were three times more likely to pursue broad operating model redesign and twice as likely to redesign workflows before selecting AI tools.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Despite $30–40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI, this report uncovers a surprising result in that 95% of organizations are getting zero return.
qs.a: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Integrated learning and coordination provide the proposed mechanisms for scalable advantage.
kps.d: Tellmann, drawing on Iansiti and Lakhani, describes an AI factory that joins data pipelines, algorithms, controlled experimentation and software infrastructure. Feedback improves services and generates further data, while modular platforms expand the range of offerings. McKinsey emphasises AI orchestration that reduces person-to-person coordination. DORA reports stronger organisational benefits where data is accessible, accurate and complete, although its excerpts provide no effect sizes. Claims that these mechanisms produce winner-takes-most markets remain strategic arguments, not demonstrated general outcomes; Tellmann also acknowledges substantial upfront investment, competitive catch-up and learning effects in traditional organisations.

qs.q: At the heart of this corporate transformation is the AI factory, a company-wide operating model built around an integrated platform of data pipelines, algorithms, and software infrastructure.

qs.q: Rather than relying on growing numbers of person-to-person interactions, AI systems can route information, decisions, and workflows through centralized orchestration layers based on clear, nonpolitical, ROIC-oriented factors or governance criteria.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The main disagreement concerns how much restructuring success requires and where initiative should originate.
kps.d: McKinsey, DORA and Tellmann stress systemic change; The GenAI Divide suggests that learning-capable systems tailored to specific processes can deliver value without major organisational restructuring. It prioritises contextual learning and workflow fit over infrastructure or talent as the core barrier, and claims employee-led personal-tool use can outperform formal programmes. That challenges the emphasis on top-down implementation, though not the shared concern with workflow integration. Urgency also varies: McKinsey stresses early-mover opportunity, whereas the Future of Professionals report explicitly accepts deliberately measured adoption aligned with organisational goals.

qs.q: Leaders must synchronise data and systems, redesign processes,  reconfigure roles and teams, and prepare people for AI-enabled ways of working, all  while ensuring that proper governance, including transparency and compliance, gets  embedded into every initiative.387  These are heavy lifts, and many organisations remain in the foothills.
qs.a: Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry · Academia · 2026

qs.q: These early results suggest that learning-capable systems, when targeted at specific processes, can deliver real value, even without major organizational restructuring.
qs.a: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Company cases illustrate possible gains without establishing universal results or inevitable job losses.
kps.d: McKinsey reports more than $120 million in documented impact and 170% ROI at Emirates Global Aluminium following a multiyear training and deployment effort. Its Toyota example compresses planning from weeks to minutes and reduces the planning team by more than 80% through redeployment, not layoffs. Freeport-McMoRan reused about 60% of its initial code across seven sites, but its hundreds of millions in EBITDA improvement remained projected. These examples support mechanisms of training, workflow compression and reuse; they do not measure legal-department outcomes. The GenAI Divide likewise reports limited layoffs and selective workforce effects rather than general headcount reductions.

qs.q: After a multiyear effort, the company ultimately documented more than $120 million in impact, including a 170 percent ROI and double-digit improvements in throughput and labor productivity.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: While most implementations don't drive headcount reduction, organizations that have crossed the GenAI Divide are beginning to see selective workforce impacts in customer support, software engineering, and administrative functions.
qs.a: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Practical recommendations converge on focused investment, business-outcome measurement and explicit human–AI responsibilities.
kps.d: McKinsey and PwC recommend concentrating senior-led investment in a few economically consequential areas, then expanding after results emerge. McKinsey sequences workflow redesign before talent planning and technology selection; The GenAI Divide favours process-specific customisation and business outcomes over software benchmarks. No more pyramids recommends classifying work as AI-only, human-plus-AI or human-only and assessing career paths, reskilling and headcount separately from effort savings. DORA recommends rewarding verification and agent orchestration. Governance remains a design requirement: McKinsey warns that agents can propagate errors through unrevised workflows, while No more pyramids reserves major decisions and accountability for people.

qs.q: But real results take precision in picking a few spots where AI can deliver wholesale transformation in ways that matter for the business, then executing with steady discipline that starts with senior leadership.
qs.a: 2026 AI Business Predictions · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The legal-industry implication is chiefly a buyer-side transformation forecast, not demonstrated legal-service disruption.
kps.d: Tellmann predicts that corporate legal departments will adopt analogous automation while people design systems, supervise their operation and set objectives and ethical guardrails. He also anticipates additional legal-team work on AI's stakeholder and governance consequences. The supplied excerpt from the corporate-legal-department catalyst article explains enterprise AI factories but does not demonstrate how legal departments catalyse industry disruption. The Big Four agents overview similarly describes scalable digital teammates and outsourcing-like efficiencies with expertise retained internally, but supplies no concrete legal-service impact evidence. These materials therefore support a proposed direction for in-house operating models, not measured changes in law-firm staffing or legal-market shares.

vlens.an: This curated academia-and-research set accepts the principal proposition that access to AI tools is insufficient and materially develops it by specifying why organisational design matters. Across the sources, scalable value depends on integrating AI into workflows, data systems and feedback loops rather than merely accelerating isolated tasks. Tellmann and the AI-factory account emphasise enterprise-wide platforms, coordinated redesign of processes and roles, and embedded governance; The GenAI Divide adds implementation evidence attributing weak returns chiefly to brittle workflows, poor contextual learning and operational misalignment. Material variation concerns the required scale and origin of change: Tellmann presents substantial, top-down organisational transformation as necessary for enterprise-wide advantage, whereas The GenAI Divide argues that process-specific, learning-capable systems—and sometimes employee-led use—can create value without major restructuring. The more expansive claims about compounding competitive advantage and winner-takes-most markets remain strategic arguments, while reported returns use differing measures and do not establish universal outcomes or demonstrated legal-sector effects.

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press sources accepts the cluster’s principal proposition and materially develops it into an implementation agenda. Across the sources, AI access and isolated task efficiencies are treated as insufficient for durable enterprise value; the recurring explanation is that gains remain trapped unless organisations redesign workflows, coordination, governance, data arrangements and talent models around business outcomes. The sources commonly recommend concentrated investment in a few consequential domains, senior or business-led execution, and explicit allocation of responsibilities between people and AI. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary strength: McKinsey offers the most systemic operating-model account, supported by survey associations and illustrative company cases but not proof of universal returns; PwC stresses focused execution while supplying mainly qualitative observations; the workforce-redesign article extends the proposition into role classification, reskilling, career paths and retained human accountability; the Future of Professionals report emphasises strategic integration and permits deliberately measured adoption; and the Big Four agents overview foregrounds scalable digital teammates, retained expertise and governance but relies largely on capability claims and forecasts. These sources therefore build on the proposition chiefly by specifying how redesign might be undertaken, while providing limited evidence of generalisable returns and little direct evidence of legal-market disruption.

qs.q: The specifics vary by industry and use case, but the sequence remains consistent: Redesign workflows first, build the supporting talent model second, and select technology third.
qs.a: The Operating Model Advantage: Why AI Winners Are Rewiring Their Organizations · Market & press · 2026

vlens.an: The legal-tech-vendor voice represented here supports the cluster’s principal proposition that organisational value depends more on redesigning work than on providing AI access alone. The DORA report argues that task-level or local gains can remain isolated, or be absorbed by an unchanged system, unless organisations alter workflows, roles, governance, incentives and feedback structures. It also identifies healthy internal data—AI-accessible, accurate and complete—as a mechanism for translating AI use into stronger organisational performance. There is no material internal disagreement because the supplied evidence contains one source. Its main qualifications concern scope and evidentiary strength: the report addresses software-development organisations rather than legal-service delivery; the supplied excerpts give no effect sizes or methodological detail for the data finding; and its AI-native workflow examples are prospective possibilities rather than demonstrated universal returns. Accordingly, it supports the proposition without establishing that redesign always produces value or that the conclusions transfer directly to legal organisations.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that broad AI access and isolated task-level productivity do not by themselves create organisation-wide value. They commonly attribute scalable returns to integration with workflows, internal context or data, governance, incentives and retained organisational expertise. The period’s material contribution is to sharpen the mechanism: the GenAI Divide identifies contextual learning and process-specific fit as central, while DORA specifies system redesign, healthy data, verification and agent orchestration. Internal variation concerns the required scale and direction of change. DORA and the Future of Professionals report emphasise coordinated, organisation-level redesign and strategy; the GenAI Divide argues that targeted learning-capable systems—and sometimes employee-led adoption—can generate value without major restructuring. The Big Four agents source is consistent with integration and governance but relies mainly on capability claims and forecasts. Reported return figures and strategy correlations use different outcomes and do not establish a common failure rate or causation, while proposed AI-native workflows remain prospective.

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that access to AI and isolated task acceleration are insufficient for enterprise transformation, and they materially develop it with operating-model and implementation frameworks. Their common reasoning is that unchanged workflows, coordination structures, data silos, governance, roles and incentives trap gains at the task level; scalable value instead requires integrated data and learning systems, workflow redesign, focused business-led investment, talent development and explicit allocation of human and AI responsibilities. Material variation concerns scope and evidential strength. PwC offers a narrower, qualitative recommendation to concentrate senior-led investment and distinguishes modest returns from transformation. McKinsey provides the most developed coordination and workflow-redesign account, supported by survey associations and illustrative company cases, while expressly treating organisational redesign as an enabling mechanism rather than value in itself. Tellmann and the corporate legal-department article extend the proposition through the AI-factory model and stronger claims about compounding or winner-takes-most advantages, but those strategic claims are not established as general outcomes; Tellmann’s legal-department implications are forecasts rather than measured legal-sector effects. “No more pyramids” adds a concrete workforce framework that preserves human decision authority and separates potential effort savings from actual headcount consequences. Thus, the period builds on the synthesis principally by specifying how redesign could work, while its cases, associations and projections do not establish universal returns.
